parents.title: Diagonal mean values and Gaussian moments of prime polynomials

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: Averaging over height acts as a controlled phase filter: after expanding the Dirichlet polynomials, the diagonal integer matches supply the main term and the off-diagonal matches enter an explicit error. For prime-supported powers, unique factorization turns those diagonal matches into a primewise Bessel product. Odd powers therefore have no diagonal main term and are only error-sized; even powers have Bessel-product diagonal moments, not yet Gaussian moments. Gaussian behavior requires a later quadratic extraction and remainder control, while the present high-moment estimate remains conditional on restrictions including N<=T and x^k<=T/log T.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: Separates a two-stage probabilistic bridge: height averaging plus arithmetic multiplicativity first yields diagonal/Bessel structure; only subsequent control of higher Bessel factors can compress that structure to a Gaussian surrogate. This locates exactly where the representation gains factorization and where the distributional proof burden remains.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Accepted after replacing the unsupported claim that odd moments vanish and removing premature Gaussian language. The revised record preserves the main-term/error distinction, the later approximation burden, and the hypotheses governing the mean- and high-moment estimates.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: Lemma 3.3 expands the height integral and isolates m=n with an off-diagonal error. accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: Calling height a phase randomizer is an interpretation of the displayed integration mechanism. parents.title: Truncating rare values before passing from moments to transforms

accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: B and B(tau) are the safety interface between polynomial moments and exponential transforms. Taylor truncation passes through that interface, while the negligible complement and Gaussian resummation reconnect the restricted analytic blocks to their probabilistic surrogate.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: The span defines the cutoff B, makes its complement very small via a high even moment and union bound, truncates the exponential series uniformly on B intersect B(tau), and removes the restriction from moments with Cauchy-Schwarz. Proposition 5.1 then evaluates the unrestricted moments and the even series resums to the one- and two-point Gaussian transforms in the stated parameter range.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: The set B bounds every retained P_j(t) at a specified power of log T, and Lemma 5.2 uses a high even moment from Proposition 5.1 plus a union bound to make B^c exponentially small on the log scale. Proposition 5.1 evaluates those moments, whose even series resums to the Gaussian transform with variance s_j^2 and covariance rho_j(tau).

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: The mesh creates enough opportunities for an extreme, but only a scale-aware second moment can certify that these opportunities are not redundant. The proof closes by showing that correlation clusters are too sparse to cancel the entropy gain.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: The random count sum_l 1_{A(tau_l)} bridges local block tails to existence of a high point. Its first moment measures opportunity, and its scale-decomposed second moment measures effective dependence; their ratio is the existence certificate.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: The span constructs about log T mesh events, evaluates the one-point probability, applies the Cauchy-Schwarz/Paley-Zygmund ratio, and splits the pair sum at the stated separation. Far pairs factor through Proposition 5.5, near pairs are stratified by m and bounded through Proposition 5.4, and lambda less than one makes the near contribution little-o of the squared first moment.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: The interval [-1/4,1/4] is divided into about log T mesh points and x_j is set to lambda log log T/K. Proposition 5.5 gives the one-point probability and hence a growing expected count of A(tau_l).
